ideas.title: 2Q algorithm was first introduced in the paper - 2Q: A low overhead high-performance buffer management replacement algorithm by Theodore Johnson and Dennis Shasha

blocks.text: In this essay, we take a detailed look into the sub-optimality of LRU and how one of its variants called 2Q addresses and improves upon it.

ideas.title: The intuition of this algorithm is so strong and implementation is so simple that until the early ’80s, LRU was the algorithm of choice in nearly all the systems

blocks.text: The LRU eviction algorithm evicts the page from the buffer which has not been accessed for the longest. LRU is typically implemented using a Doubly Linked List and a Hash Table. But as stated above, there are certain situations where LRU performs sub-optimal.

ideas.title: If these pages are not referenced again, this is a total loss and the performance of the database takes a massive hit

blocks.text: If the database table is bigger than the LRU cache, the DB process, upon scanning the table will wipe out the entire LRU cache and fill it with the pages from just one scanned table. The performance will pickup once these pages are evicted from the cache and other pages make an entry.

ideas.title: 2Q also considers access frequency while making the decision to ensure the page that is really warm gets a place in the LRU cache

blocks.text: 2Q addresses the above-illustrated issues by introducing parallel buffers and supporting queues. It admits only hot pages to the main buffer and tests every page for a second reference.

ideas.title: The golden rule that 2Q is based on is - *Just because a page is accessed once does not entitle it to stay in the buffer

blocks.text: Instead, it should be decided if it is accessed again then only keep it in the buffer.*

ideas.title: An AI workflow is a dependency graph, not a list
ideas.section: The Dependency Problem in AI Workflows
ideas.takeaway: If you cannot draw the edges, you cannot know what can run in parallel or what a failure affects.

blocks.text: Every workflow has producers and consumers, and consumers cannot run before their inputs exist. A DAG models tasks as nodes and dependencies as directed edges; topological sort turns that graph into a valid execution order.

ideas.title: Dependencies are correctness constraints, not scheduling preferences
ideas.section: The Dependency Problem in AI Workflows
ideas.takeaway: Running a step early does not save time; it reads stale data or calls a tool with missing context.

blocks.text: Embedding before chunking embeds dirty text. Retrieving before the index is complete queries an incomplete index. The edges are not optional; they are the difference between a correct pipeline and a plausible-looking one.

ideas.title: Let the graph find parallelism
ideas.takeaway: Nodes in the same topological level have no dependency between them and can run concurrently.

blocks.text: In a branching RAG pipeline, keyword filtering and retrieval can run in parallel once the index is built; the merge node waits for both. Topological sort produces the order automatically, so the orchestrator does not hardcode sequencing.

ideas.title: Recompute only the affected subgraph
ideas.takeaway: On failure or input change, traverse forward from the affected node and reuse every cached output outside it.

blocks.text: This is how Bazel and Buck avoid rebuilding the world. The DAG makes it tractable: without explicit dependency edges, you cannot know which downstream nodes are affected.

ideas.title: Topological sort does not balance work
ideas.takeaway: It tells you the order, not where the critical path is.

blocks.text: If ten parallel tasks feed one merge node, the merge waits for the slowest. Profile the longest chain of dependent tasks to see where parallelism actually helps; fan-in bottlenecks remain.

ideas.title: Validate cycles at definition time, not at 2 AM
ideas.takeaway: A cycle means deadlock: A waits for B, B waits for A, nothing progresses.

blocks.text: If the topological order is shorter than the graph, there is a cycle. Catch it when the workflow is defined, surface the offending cycle, and reject the workflow before a single task runs.

items: Compare the topological order length with the node count.
Identify the nodes that remain in the cycle.
Reject the workflow at definition time.
Show a clear error instead of hanging at runtime.

ideas.title: A DAG is a contract
ideas.takeaway: The graph is the spec; the topological order is the scheduler's input.

blocks.text: Drawing the dependency graph first forces you to separate truly sequential tasks from independent ones. Parallelism, cycle safety and incremental recomputation all fall out of the structure you declared.

ideas.title: G-Eval turns an LLM into a rubric-driven judge
ideas.takeaway: Use it when output quality is real but there is no single gold answer to compare against.

blocks.text: G-Eval is a prompting framework for reference-free evaluation. It gives a model a precise rubric, lets it generate its own evaluation steps, and converts its token probabilities into a fine-grained score instead of trusting a printed digit.

ideas.title: Reference-free evaluation is the point
ideas.takeaway: Most real outputs—support replies, summaries, chatbot turns—have no one correct answer in a dataset.

blocks.text: A reference-based metric needs a gold-standard example. G-Eval does not. It defines the dimension precisely and asks the judge to evaluate the candidate against that definition, which is why it can cover custom criteria like brand voice or refund-policy compliance.

ideas.title: Make the rubric precise, not a 1–5 vibe check
ideas.takeaway: A vague rubric collapses to "does this look fine"; a precise one gives the judge specific things to check.

blocks.text: Instead of "rate this 1 to 5", define what coherence means in concrete terms. A vague rubric gives the model nothing to anchor against, so it cannot discriminate a mediocre output from a strong one. A precise rubric is also what makes human raters consistent.

ideas.title: Generate the evaluation chain-of-thought once per rubric
ideas.takeaway: Commit to a procedure before seeing outputs, then cache it.

blocks.text: G-Eval asks the model to write its own evaluation steps from the task and criterion before it sees a candidate. That forces a concrete procedure instead of pattern-matching, and leaves an audit trail: when a score looks wrong, read the chain-of-thought to see where the judge diverged.

ideas.title: Never judge with the same model family
ideas.section: The Bias You Need to Know About
ideas.takeaway: LLM judges show a measurable self-preference bias toward their own family.

blocks.text: Even when human reviewers prefer the alternative, judges favor text generated by models from their own family. Use a different family for the judge than for the system under test, pin the judge version, and recalibrate the rubric against human-labeled examples.

ideas.title: Use a classifier or parser when the answer is closed-form
ideas.section: When This Is the Wrong Tool
ideas.takeaway: G-Eval is the wrong tool for toxicity, PII or valid JSON.

blocks.text: Anything with a sharp, closed-form answer does not need a reasoning model reading a rubric. A fast classifier or parser is cheaper, faster and more reliable. Reach for G-Eval only when the judgment is open-ended.

ideas.title: The RUM Conjecture states that we cannot design an access method for a storage system that is optimal in all the following three aspects - Reads, Updates, and, Memory

blocks.text: The conjecture puts forth that we always have to trade one to make the other two optimal and this makes the three constitutes a competing triangle, very similar to the famous CAP theorem.

ideas.title: An ideal storage system would be the one that has an access method that provides lowest Read Overhead, minimal Update Cost

blocks.text: In the real-world, achieving this is near impossible and that is something that is dictated by this conjecture.

ideas.title: Memory Overhead is measured through Space Amplification and it is defined as the ratio between the space utilized for auxiliary and main data and space utilized by the main data

blocks.text: Read Overhead is measured through Read Amplification and it is defined as the ratio between the total amount of data read (main + auxiliary) and the amount of main data intended to be read.

ideas.title: To be memory-optimized the systems usually use compress the main data and auxiliary storages, or allow some error rate, like false positives

blocks.text: Memory Optimised storage systems are designed to minimize auxiliary memory required for access and updates on the main data.

ideas.title: Slop debt is incoherence, not technical debt at volume
ideas.takeaway: The danger of LLM-generated code is not how much there is; it is that nobody chose its shape.

blocks.text: Slop debt is what accumulates when most of a codebase is generated by an LLM, reviewed by nobody who understands it, and merged because the tests pass. It compiles and works for now, but it was predicted one plausible token at a time rather than designed.

ideas.title: Tech debt comes from a decision; slop debt comes from the absence of one
ideas.section: Why It Is Not The Same Thing
ideas.takeaway: A decision leaves a reason you can recover. Slop leaves no author to ask.

blocks.text: Classic tech debt is a tradeoff: skip the abstraction, hardcode a value, ship now. The reason survives in the person or the git history. Slop debt has no architect; the model chose the variable names and error handling independently for every file, with no memory of the last one.

ideas.title: Slop debt compounds because the model reads its own slop
ideas.takeaway: Every generation pass turns existing incoherence into context for the next pass.

blocks.text: Once a codebase has hundreds of files of locally correct but globally inconsistent code, the next generation pass uses that code as context. It copies the bad abstraction because that is what it sees, and adds a third error-handling style because it cannot tell which of the first two is intended.

ideas.title: Code review cannot catch slop because slop is plausible
ideas.section: The Point Where Debugging Stops Working
ideas.takeaway: Reviewers pattern-match on plausibility; slop is wrong in how it fits, not in how it reads.

blocks.text: A slop diff reads correctly. It is only wrong in the way it fails to fit with everything around it, and that kind of wrong does not show up in a line-by-line diff. The person who "wrote" it clicked accept.

ideas.title: Incremental refactoring does not fix smeared incoherence
ideas.section: Why Refactoring Does Not Save You
ideas.takeaway: Tech debt is local; slop debt is everywhere at low intensity.

blocks.text: The normal move for tech debt is to isolate a module, test it, clean it up and move on. Slop debt has no single module to point at. Cleaning one file does not reduce the system's confusion while the file next to it generates new confusion at the same rate.

ideas.title: Past a certain size, rewrite with a human-owned architecture
ideas.takeaway: At scale, the honest fix is not "clean it up" but "start over with a shape a human chose".

blocks.text: Once slop debt has metastasized, refactoring cannot restore coherence. The workable reset is a rewrite where a human makes the architectural calls and the model is used as a tool inside a shape someone designed, not as the designer.

items: Stop treating it as high-volume tech debt.
Accept that incremental cleanup will not reduce system-wide confusion.
Budget for a rewrite once incoherence is smeared across the codebase.
Keep a human in charge of architecture and use the model as an implementation tool.

ideas.title: Most engineers encounter cardinality estimation the same way: they get paged because a `COUNT` query is killing the database, and someone suggests HyperLogLog

blocks.text: HLL solves the “how many unique things” problem elegantly, and for a large class of systems that is enough. But then the analytics team asks something different: “How many users saw campaign A but not campaign B?” or “What is the overlap between users who clicked this ad and users who made a purchase?” Suddenly HLL stops being enough. You need set algebra over streams, and that is where Theta sketches earn their place.

ideas.title: A hash set of 100 million 64-bit user IDs costs roughly 800 MB, and that is before you account for load factors and memory fragmentation in real hash table implementations
ideas.section: The problem that cardinality sketches solve

blocks.text: At small scale, counting distinct elements is a solved problem. Load the data into memory, use a hash set, and read off the size. At large scale this falls apart fast.

ideas.title: By filtering both sets to the minimum theta, you ensure that elements below the threshold were subject to the same sampling decision in both sketches, making the set operations meaningful
ideas.section: Set operations: the thing that makes Theta sketches irreplaceable

blocks.text: The critical property that makes this all work is that the hash function is deterministic and universal. If a user appears in both stream A and stream B, their ID hashes to the same value in both sketches. Whether they appear in S_A depends on whether hash(user_id) < theta_A.

ideas.title: Systems that need to report confidence intervals should always call `getUpperBound` and `getLowerBound` rather than just `getEstimate`

blocks.text: This matters for systems that pre-compute and store sketches. If a sketch is in exact mode, you know the estimate is precise. If it is in estimation mode, you apply the RSE guarantee.

ideas.title: Only 0.1% of elements are retained

blocks.text: The intuition is clear: intersection works by finding common hash values below the minimum theta. If the intersection has only 1000 elements, you expect to retain roughly 1 element in the intersection sketch. Estimating a population from a single sample has enormous variance.

ideas.title: The moment you introduce a custom seed — perhaps for security reasons, to prevent hash flooding
ideas.section: The seed problem and why you cannot ignore it

blocks.text: The DataSketches library uses a default seed of 9001. If you use the default everywhere, this is not a problem.

ideas.title: Old sketches hashed with the old seed cannot participate in set operations with new sketches using a new seed
ideas.section: The seed problem and why you cannot ignore it

blocks.text: Also: do not change the seed after you have stored sketches. There is no migration path.

ideas.title: The tradeoff is that Tuple sketches are larger than plain Theta sketches, proportional to the size of the summary data stored per entry

blocks.text: The Theta sketch family includes an extension called Tuple sketches. A Tuple sketch attaches a summary object to each retained hash entry.

ideas.title: Given a sketch, you cannot determine whether a specific element was in the original stream
ideas.section: When not to use Theta sketches

blocks.text: Theta sketches cannot answer membership queries. The retained hash values are deterministic but the sketch does not store which original elements produced them (for large inputs with small theta, most elements are dropped entirely). If you need probabilistic membership testing, Bloom filters are the right tool.

ideas.title: The cost grows linearly with the number of sketches, not with the cardinality of the data they represent

blocks.text: Each retained entry is a 64-bit long (8 bytes). At k = 4096 with the default compact format, a sketch uses roughly 32 KB plus a small fixed header. At k = 16384, that is 128 KB plus header.

ideas.title: Docs rot silently; tools fail loudly
ideas.section: Why Build Tools Instead of Writing Docs
ideas.takeaway: Encode operational knowledge as executable tools, not prose nobody notices is stale.

blocks.text: A stale wiki can mislead people for months. A broken tool fails in front of the next person who uses it, which means it actually gets fixed. That difference matters more now that AI agents act on the same instructions.

ideas.title: The three skills are create-service, deploy and debug
ideas.section: Why Build Tools Instead of Writing Docs
ideas.takeaway: These are the three places where missing knowledge turns into waiting, guessing and 2 AM incidents.

blocks.text: The article's three skills: provision a new service end to end, deploy and roll back with tests and smoke checks, and diagnose an incident from symptoms to evidence. Each turns a manual, stale process into an executable one.

ideas.title: Build the debugging skill first
ideas.takeaway: Incidents happen on their own schedule, so every one can add a verified failure pattern.

blocks.text: The debugging skill should match live symptoms to known failure patterns for that service, link directly to the relevant logs, traces and dashboards, and run diagnostics instead of pointing at raw data. Start with the service that pages most and takes longest to fix.

items: Keep a running incident history per service.
Link dependencies and their health dashboards.
Extract verified failure patterns from retros.
Return a likely cause, evidence and links—not "check the logs".

ideas.title: Build deployment second, with rollback and smoke tests
ideas.takeaway: Rollback is the path used under pressure and the one most teams exercise least.

blocks.text: The deployment skill should run tests against the real target environment, roll out gradually, execute smoke tests automatically, and roll back without a human remembering a separate procedure. It needs deployment history, migration state, environment config and a defined set of smoke-test endpoints.

items: Test against the real target environment.
Roll out gradually.
Run smoke tests automatically.
Roll back on failure without a separate manual runbook.

ideas.title: Build create-service last
ideas.takeaway: It touches the most infrastructure; a half-built version is worse than none.

blocks.text: The create-service skill provisions the database, wires logging, registers identity and deploys to production before anyone writes business logic. It is the most valuable day-one fix, but also the riskiest to half-build because it relocates confusion instead of removing it.

ideas.title: Track one metric per tool
ideas.takeaway: Pick a number that is cheap to measure and hard to argue with.

blocks.text: Measure time from a fresh repo to a live deployment, deployment frequency alongside rollback rate, and mean time to diagnose an incident. Feed incidents and rough onboarding experiences back into the tools as requirements.

blocks.text: In order to make sense of such an irregular plot and find a pattern or a trend out of it, we have to get rid of **short-term irregularities** without substantial information loss; and this process is called “smoothing”.

ideas.section: Time Series and need of Smoothing

blocks.text: The technique we used to smooth the temperature plot is known as Simple Moving Average (SMA) and it is the simplest, most effective, and one of the most popular smoothing techniques for time series data. Moving Average, very instinctively, smooths out short-term irregularities and highlights longer-term trends and patterns.

ideas.title: SMA ensures that there is no substantial loss of data resolution in the smoothened plot
ideas.section: Time Series Smoothing using Moving Average

blocks.text: The technique we used to smooth the temperature plot is known as Simple Moving Average (SMA) and it is the simplest, most effective, and one of the most popular smoothing techniques for time series data. Moving Average, very instinctively, smooths out short-term irregularities and highlights longer-term trends and patterns. Computing it is also very simple - each point in the smoothened plot is just an unweighted mean of the data points lying in the sliding window of length `n`.

ideas.title: Simple Moving Average is a very effective smoothing technique but choosing the optimal window size is a challenge

blocks.text: Picking a smaller window size will not help in getting rid of irregularities while picking the window size that is too large will mask all the anomalies.

ideas.title: In any data distribution, the anomalies and aberrations form in the long tail which means they are some extreme values that are far away from the mean

blocks.text: Being part of the long tail makes these anomalies - outliers i.e. data points that do not really fit the distribution.

ideas.title: Finding the global optimal window size, that maximizes Kurtosis, is not always a good idea, because doing so can totally distort the plot leading to heavy information loss

blocks.text: A better way is to find local optimum within pre-defined limits; for example, an optimal point for window size between 10 and 40. These limits totally depend on the data at hand. Doing this not only leads to a smooth plot that highlights anomalies but also converges the computation to a local optimum much quicker.
